metaDescription: Radon test before buying a house? A 91-day test won't fit most closings. What a short-term screen shows, what to test after possession. Call (204) 555-0173.
h1: Radon Test Before Buying a House in Manitoba or Saskatchewan
heroSub: A proper radon test runs at least 91 days, and most closings don't wait that long. Here's what a screening test can tell you during the sale, what it can't, and how to finish the job once you have the keys.
introHtml:
A radon test before buying a house sounds simple until you look at the calendar. Health Canada's guideline is 200 Bq/m3 (becquerels per cubic metre, a measure of radioactivity in the air), and it applies to the average level over a year. The shortest test Health Canada accepts for comparing a home against it runs 91 days. If your closing is 30 days out, that test does not fit.

So the realistic plan has two parts. During the sale, a short-term screening test or a continuous digital monitor gives you a rough read, and C-NRPP (the Canadian National Radon Proficiency Program) says a short-term screening "could be conducted to provide some insight". After possession you run a long-term test and base any decision on that number. Call (204) 555-0173 and we'll put you in touch with an independent C-NRPP certified measurement professional who works in Winnipeg, Regina, Saskatoon or the towns around them.

features.title: Short-term screening during the condition period
features.desc: A certified measurement professional can run a short-term screen while the offer is still conditional. It tells you roughly where the house sits, but Health Canada says short-term results are not the basis for a mitigation decision.

features.title: Continuous digital monitors
features.desc: Electronic monitors log readings across the test instead of giving one number at the end. During a sale they are screening tools; if you later use one for a long-term test, Health Canada says pick one on C-NRPP's approved list.

features.title: Placement that holds up
features.desc: The detector goes in the lowest lived-in level, in the breathing zone at least 30 cm above the floor and 30 cm from walls. Keep it away from sumps, vents, windows and heat sources, or the result means very little.

features.title: Long-term test after possession
features.desc: At least 91 days, with 91 of them in the heating season; 3 to 12 months is better. HomeRadonTest.ca sells a kit for $70.00 before tax, with shipping both ways and the lab analysis included.

features.title: Seller-side testing done early
features.desc: A seller who starts a long-term test months before listing has a real annual-average number to hand a buyer. That usually beats a rushed screen run in the middle of the deal.

features.title: Checking a house that already has a system
features.desc: If there's a pipe and fan in the basement, the fan should be running and the U-tube manometer should show a level difference between its two sides. Ask the seller for the test result taken after the system went in.

sections.heading: Why a 91-day radon test doesn't fit a home sale
sections.html:
Health Canada recommends a long-term test of at least 3 months, with a minimum of 91 days in the heating season. The reason is that the 200 Bq/m3 guideline is an annual average, and a few days of data can land well above or below it. Health Canada is blunt about it: "short-term measurements are not appropriate for informing mitigation decisions."

That leaves buyers with a gap. Most purchase timelines are measured in weeks, and you can't leave a detector in someone else's basement for three months. A short-term screen is the tool that fits the window, as long as everyone understands it is a first look and not the final answer.

Is it worth doing at all? Radon is common here. In the 2024 Cross-Canada survey, roughly 1 in 3 of the tested homes in Saskatchewan and Manitoba were at or above 200 Bq/m3; that figure is unweighted, and Health Canada says no area of Canada is radon-free. A screen during the sale won't settle the question, but it can tell you whether to expect a mitigation bill.

sections.heading: What a screening test can and can't tell you
sections.html:
There are three classes of equipment you'll run into during a sale. Each has a job, and each can go wrong in predictable ways.

  • Short-term professional screening: quick, done while the deal is conditional, useful as a flag. Not a basis for a mitigation decision.
  • Continuous digital monitors: log readings over time. Library loaners fall here; Winnipeg Public Library lends them at every branch from 1 November to 30 April on a three-week loan, and CBC reported that each monitor should sit in the lowest level for at least seven days. You'd need the seller's permission to set one up in their house.
  • Passive long-term kits: placed for 91 days or more, then mailed to a lab. Kits sold through HomeRadonTest.ca are analysed by the Saskatchewan Research Council lab. This is the test that counts, and it belongs after possession.

The common failure modes are placement ones. A detector sitting next to the sump, a floor vent or an open window, or placed in a crawl space, furnace room or unfinished storage area, is not measuring the air your family will breathe. A device that got moved or unplugged partway through is another. Ask whoever runs the test where they put it and why.

sections.heading: Conditions, holdbacks and disclosure: questions for your realtor or lawyer
sections.html:
We could not find any Manitoba or Saskatchewan rule that requires radon testing or radon disclosure when a house is sold. In Saskatchewan, a property condition disclosure statement is not required for a sale, but sellers must tell buyers about defects they know of that a reasonable inspection wouldn't find. In Manitoba, the Property Disclosure Statement is Appendix A to the residential offer to purchase; whether it asks about radon is something your realtor can confirm.

Health Canada says real estate licensees have professional duties that include disclosing radon as a known latent defect. If a seller has a test result, it's fair to ask for it.

How you handle radon in the deal is a legal and negotiating question, and this page is not legal advice. Things worth raising with your realtor or lawyer:

  • A condition that lets you run a short-term screen before the offer goes firm.
  • A holdback of part of the price until a long-term result comes in after closing.
  • Using a written quote from a C-NRPP certified mitigation professional as the basis for a price conversation.
  • Whether the seller's existing test result or system paperwork forms part of the sale.

sections.heading: After possession: the long-term test and what comes next
sections.html:
Start a long-term test once you move in, ideally before the heating season so you get the full 91 days of it. Place it in the lowest level you actually live in. If you finish the basement later and it becomes the lowest lived-in level, Health Canada says to test again. The Manitoba government puts kit prices at "between $50 and $100".

Health Canada lists radon as the leading cause of lung cancer in non-smokers and the second leading cause overall. That's the reason to test, not a reason to panic. If your result is over 200 Bq/m3, Health Canada recommends fixing it within 1 year, usually with sub-slab depressurization installed by a C-NRPP certified mitigation professional. The 200 figure is a guideline, not a legal limit, and no province requires a homeowner to act on it.

On cost, Winnipeg installers advertise systems from about $1,500 to $3,000; a Regina installer quotes $2,500 to $3,500. The mitigation cost page breaks those down. In Manitoba, the Manitoba Hydro Home Energy Efficiency Loan covers radon mitigation up to $5,000, and the Lungs Matter program offers up to $1,500 to low- or moderate-income households. In Saskatchewan, Lung Saskatchewan has offered reimbursement in the past; check its site for the current status.

faq.q: Can I get a radon test done before my closing date?
faq.a: You can get a screening done, but not the test that counts. Health Canada's minimum is 91 days in the heating season, which won't fit inside a 30-day closing. A short-term screen or continuous monitor during the condition period gives you a rough read, and a long-term test after possession gives you the real number.

faq.q: Is a short-term radon result good enough to negotiate on?
faq.a: Health Canada says short-term results are not appropriate for mitigation decisions, so treat one as a flag rather than a verdict. If a screen comes back high, a written quote from a C-NRPP certified mitigation professional gives you something concrete: Winnipeg installers advertise systems from about $1,500 to $3,000, and a Regina installer quotes $2,500 to $3,500. How to use that in the deal is a question for your realtor or lawyer.

faq.q: Does a seller in Manitoba or Saskatchewan have to disclose radon?
faq.a: We found no Manitoba or Saskatchewan rule that specifically requires radon testing or disclosure at sale. In Saskatchewan, sellers must disclose known defects that a reasonable inspection wouldn't reveal, and Health Canada says real estate licensees should disclose radon as a known latent defect. Your lawyer can tell you how that applies to your deal.

faq.q: The house already has a radon system. What should I check?
faq.a: The fan should be running, since Health Canada says it must run continuously to work. The U-tube manometer on the pipe should show a level difference between its two sides. Ask the seller for the post-install test result, then run your own long-term test of at least 91 days after you move in; Health Canada's 2014 national figure for a replacement fan is $200 to $300 if the old one has failed.

faq.q: What does a long-term radon test cost after we move in?
faq.a: HomeRadonTest.ca sells a single-use long-term kit for $70.00 before tax, including shipping both ways and the lab analysis, and the Manitoba government puts kits at between $50 and $100. Free digital screening monitors are on loan at Winnipeg Public Library from 1 November to 30 April, and Moose Jaw Public Library lends them from 1 October to 1 April. Those loaners are for screening; the 91-day test is still the one to act on.
